# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Gleidesk Renewables Acquisition Corp. – Acquisition of Tenein Rooftop Solar, Inc.: Issues List for Pre-Closing Attention

---

## 1. Bottom Line

The SPA was signed on October 20, 2026 and has not closed. That gives Gleidesk time, and some leverage, to fix four problems before Closing. In order of significance:

1. **Uncapped Buyer indemnity that reaches pre-Closing installations.** Gleidesk has, in effect, agreed to give Seller an *unlimited* indemnity for the Company's pre-Closing workmanship, roof-penetration and production warranty exposure. That exposure is meant to sit with Seller under Section 9.2(d).
2. **The Fresno warehouse renewal window closed on October 2, 2026, before signing.** Seller cannot perform the Section 6.4 renewal covenant. The Company's principal warehouse lease expires March 31, 2027, with no renewal right left.
3. **The Bill of Sale caps title claims on the Transferred Assets.** Through SPA Section 11.12, this displaces the Fundamental Representation carve-out. Title claims on the vehicles, inventory and equipment become capped at $4,850,000 and share that cap with every other general claim.
4. **The Bill of Sale chooses California law and Fresno County courts.** Through the same Section 11.12, this splits disputes over the Transferred Assets away from the SPA's Delaware law and Court of Chancery forum.

Points 1, 3 and 4 need a written amendment signed by all parties (SPA Section 11.6), because the Bill of Sale form is an exhibit to the executed SPA. Point 2 gives Gleidesk real leverage to get that amendment. Seller's inability to perform Section 6.4 puts the Section 7.2(b) closing condition at risk and may support termination rights under Section 8.1(c).

**Key deal figures:**
- Purchase Price: $48,500,000 (SPA §2.1).
- Seller Cap: 10% of the Purchase Price, or $4,850,000 (SPA §9.4(a)).
- Deductible: $485,000 (SPA §9.4(c)).
- The Cap does not apply to Fundamental Representations (§§4.1, 4.2 and 4.6) or Fraud. Those claims are capped at the Purchase Price, except Fraud (SPA §9.4(b)).
- Governing law: Delaware (SPA §11.8). Exclusive forum: Delaware Court of Chancery (SPA §11.9).
- General reps survive 18 months after Closing (SPA §9.1).
- Outside date: January 31, 2027 (SPA §8.1(b)).

---

## 2. Issues, Ranked by Significance

### Issue 1 — Buyer's uncapped indemnity for "Assumed Warranty Obligations" covers pre-Closing installations

**Location:**
- SPA Section 9.3(c): Buyer indemnifies Seller for Losses arising from "the Assumed Warranty Obligations, as defined in Schedule 4.12 of the Disclosure Schedule".
- SPA Section 9.4(d): "Buyer's obligations under Section 9.3(c) shall not be subject to the Cap or the Deductible".
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.12, para. 9.2: defines Assumed Warranty Obligations as all workmanship, roof-penetration and production warranty obligations "for installations whether completed before or after the Closing Date."

**What the documents do:**
- Section 9.2(d) makes Seller responsible, subject to the Cap, for warranty claims "arising out of an installation completed by the Company before the Closing Date."
- Section 9.3(c), read with the Schedule 4.12 definition, makes Gleidesk responsible to Seller for the same pre-Closing warranty obligations, with no cap and no deductible.
- The SPA incorporates the Schedule definition by reference. The Section 11.12 precedence clause therefore does not help: no Ancillary Document is in conflict, because the SPA itself imports the definition.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **It can unwind Seller's warranty indemnity.** If Gleidesk recovers from Seller under Section 9.2(d) for a pre-Closing defect, Seller can argue that its payment is a "Loss arising out of" an Assumed Warranty Obligation. Seller would then claim it straight back under Section 9.3(c). At best this produces a circular dispute. At worst, Section 9.2(d) has no economic value. The same argument could reach Section 9.2(a) claims under the Section 4.12 workmanlike-installation rep.
- **The exposure is unlimited and large.** Schedule 4.12 discloses:
  - about 6,120 residential and 214 commercial installations still in warranty;
  - 1,480 Performance Plus systems with 10-year production guarantees;
  - total warranty cost rising from $611,400 (2023) to $902,300 (2025), with $688,100 through September 30, 2026;
  - a known flashing-sealant defect on about 140 2024 installations, only about 60 of them remediated.
- **It also covers direct claims against Seller.** Any customer or third-party claim against Seller arising from pre-Closing work, such as a veil-piercing or successor theory, would also be Gleidesk's uncapped responsibility.
- **It appears to have been added late.** The superseded September 24 Buyer draft has no Section 9.3(c) and no second sentence in Section 9.4(d). That draft is not operative and has no legal effect. It is useful negotiation history, and it suggests the provision was a Seller insertion and not a Buyer-agreed allocation. **We need the client and deal team to confirm how and when this language entered the signed version.**

**Recommended fix (in order of preference):**
1. Amend Schedule 4.12 para. 9.2 so that Assumed Warranty Obligations covers only installations **completed after the Closing Date**.
2. Add an express statement that Section 9.3(c) does not apply to any matter for which Seller is responsible under Section 9.2(d) or Section 9.2(a), and that Section 9.2 controls in any conflict.
3. Make Buyer's Section 9.3(c) obligation subject to a cap, for example the same $4,850,000 Cap, or delete it entirely. Post-Closing warranty obligations belong to the Company, which Gleidesk will own anyway, so a Buyer indemnity in Seller's favour serves little legitimate purpose.

**Judgment call:** Seller may argue that the parties deliberately agreed to this allocation in exchange for price. We should ask the client whether there was any such discussion before taking a hard position.

---

### Issue 2 — Fresno warehouse renewal deadline passed before signing; Section 6.4 cannot be performed

**Location:**
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.10(a), para. 8.1(d), (f) and (g).
- SPA Section 6.4.

**What the documents show:**
- The Fresno Warehouse Lease with Pellucid Logistics Park LLC expires **March 31, 2027**.
- The single 5-year renewal option must be exercised by written notice "no later than one hundred eighty (180) days before the lease expiration date". If notice is not timely, the option lapses.
- 180 days before March 31, 2027 is **October 2, 2026**.
- The Schedule, dated October 20, 2026, states that "no renewal notice has been delivered."
- The SPA was signed on **October 20, 2026**, 18 days after the deadline. Section 6.4 nevertheless requires Seller, before Closing, to "cause the Company to exercise the renewal option ... in accordance with its terms." By its terms, the option had already lapsed when Seller gave that covenant.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **This is the Company's core facility.** Schedule 4.10(a) describes the Fresno Warehouse as the Company's principal inventory storage, fleet staging and dispatch facility. It also houses the Transferred Assets: about $1.18M of inventory, the forklifts and the racking.
- **The lease will run out soon after Closing.** If Closing happens near the January 31, 2027 outside date, the Company will have about two months of term left and no contractual renewal right. Any extension will be on whatever terms Pellucid chooses to offer.
- **There is likely no rep claim.** The lapse is disclosed against Section 4.10, so Gleidesk probably cannot bring a rep-based indemnity claim.
- **A covenant claim is uncertain.** A claim under Section 9.2(b) for breach of Section 6.4 is possible. Seller will argue that performance was impossible at signing and that Gleidesk signed with the disclosure in hand. Whether Gleidesk can recover relocation costs on that basis is uncertain.
- **Gleidesk has leverage now.** It has not closed or waived anything:
  - Failure to perform Section 6.4 should cause the Section 7.2(b) condition (covenants performed in all material respects) to fail.
  - Gleidesk may have a termination right under Section 8.1(c), after written notice and the 20-day cure period.
  - Section 6.6 confirms that Seller's notice of a problem does not cure a breach.

**Recommended fix (to be pursued before Closing):**
1. **Preferred:** require, as an express closing condition added by amendment, a **landlord-signed lease amendment or extension** from Pellucid. It should extend the term on acceptable terms, ideally five years at the original 95%-of-FMR economics. It should also include landlord consent or estoppel confirming no default.
2. **Fallback, if Pellucid will not extend:** a **special, uncapped and deductible-free indemnity** from Seller for relocation costs, increased rent and business-interruption losses, backed by an escrow or holdback from the Purchase Price. Alternatively, a price reduction.
3. Replace Section 6.4 with a covenant that can actually be performed, for example "Seller shall cause the Company to use reasonable best efforts to obtain from Pellucid a written extension on the terms set out in [Annex]," with the condition above tied to it.
4. Reserve Gleidesk's rights in writing now. A notice under Sections 6.6 and 8.1(c) protects the condition and the termination right without committing Gleidesk to walk away.

**Facts we need from the client:**
- Has anyone approached Pellucid? Is the landlord willing to extend, and on what terms?
- Does the actual lease (Industrial Lease Agreement dated March 15, 2022, as amended January 9, 2024, in the data room) compute the 180-day period, or treat late notice, differently from the Schedule summary? Under para. 1.4, the Schedule summary is qualified by the underlying document.
- Did the client know of the lapse at signing? This affects how hard we can push on a covenant-breach theory.
- What alternative facilities exist in Fresno, and what would relocation realistically cost? This sizes the indemnity or escrow.

---

### Issue 3 — Bill of Sale makes title claims "subject to the Cap," overriding the Fundamental Representation carve-out

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale (Exhibit B), Section 4.3.
- Read with SPA Sections 4.6, 9.4(a), 9.4(b) and 11.12.

**What the documents do:**
- SPA Section 4.6 (Title to Transferred Assets) is a Fundamental Representation. Under Section 9.4(b), the $4,850,000 Cap and the $485,000 Deductible do not apply to breaches of it. Recovery runs up to the full Purchase Price.
- Bill of Sale Section 4.3 states that Seller's liability for breach of the Bill of Sale title warranties "is subject to the Cap set forth in Section 9.4(a) of the Purchase Agreement."
- SPA Section 11.12 provides that in any conflict between the SPA and an Ancillary Document, "the Bill of Sale controls as to the Transferred Assets; otherwise this Agreement controls."
- Bill of Sale Section 6 states that the Bill of Sale is subject to the SPA "as provided in Section 11.12." That simply points back to the clause that lets the Bill of Sale win.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **The carve-out is likely lost for these assets.** Seller will argue that, for the vehicles, inventory and warehouse equipment, the Bill of Sale cap controls and displaces the Section 9.4(b) carve-out. On that reading, title claims are limited to $4,850,000.
- **Title claims would draw down the shared Cap.** The Cap is an aggregate limit for all Section 9.2(a) and 9.2(d) claims. Every title loss would reduce the capacity left for ordinary rep breaches and pre-Closing warranty claims. Given the warranty claims history in Issue 1, that capacity is likely to be needed.
- **The exposure is not limited to asset value.** The allocated value of the Transferred Assets is about $2.6M (Schedule 2.4). Losses from undisclosed liens, competing ownership claims or loss of use of the fleet and inventory could still be significant.

**Judgment call:** One could argue there is no "conflict." The Bill of Sale warranty is a separate instrument, and the SPA Section 4.6 claim remains uncapped. We should not rely on that. The precedence clause is drafted broadly ("as to the Transferred Assets"), and Seller has a straightforward textual argument.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend Bill of Sale Section 4.3 to state that claims for breach of the title warranties are Fundamental Representation claims. They should not be subject to the Cap or the Deductible, consistent with SPA Section 9.4(b).
- In addition, amend SPA Section 11.12 so the SPA controls in all respects, with the Bill of Sale controlling only the mechanics of conveyance (for example, DMV transfer documentation).

---

### Issue 4 — Bill of Sale selects California law and Fresno County courts, splitting the forum

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale (Exhibit B), Section 7.1 (California law) and Section 7.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of the state courts in Fresno County, California).
- Read with SPA Sections 11.8, 11.9 and 11.12.

**What the documents do:**
- The SPA is governed by **Delaware law** (Section 11.8). It submits all disputes "arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the transactions contemplated by it" to the exclusive jurisdiction of the **Delaware Court of Chancery** (Section 11.9).
- The Bill of Sale chooses California law for all claims relating to it "or to the sale, conveyance and transfer of the Transferred Assets." It submits those claims exclusively to the Fresno County state courts.
- Because Section 11.12 makes the Bill of Sale control "as to the Transferred Assets," Seller can argue the California clauses govern.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **One dispute could run in two forums.** A dispute over a defective title or undisclosed lien on a vehicle may be litigated in Fresno under California law. The related indemnity claim under Article IX (for example, a Section 4.6 claim or the Cap fight in Issue 3) would belong in Delaware Chancery under Delaware law. Gleidesk could face parallel proceedings, inconsistent results, higher costs and arguments over which exclusive forum clause wins.
- **The jury waiver may not hold in California.** The SPA's jury waiver (Section 11.10) may not be enforced in a California forum, because California courts generally refuse to enforce pre-dispute contractual jury waivers. California litigation counsel should confirm this.

**Recommended fix:**
- Conform Bill of Sale Section 7 to SPA Sections 11.8–11.9: Delaware law and exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, with the same fallback courts and jury waiver.
- Keep a narrow carve-out allowing California DMV and other registration filings to be made under California procedures.
- Make the same Section 11.12 amendment proposed in Issue 3.

---

## 3. Recommended Next Steps for the Client Conversation

1. **Package the fixes into one SPA amendment** under Section 11.6. It would cover:
   - narrowing Schedule 4.12 and capping or deleting Section 9.3(c) and the second sentence of Section 9.4(d) (Issue 1);
   - replacing Section 6.4 and adding a landlord-extension closing condition or a special indemnity with escrow (Issue 2);
   - conforming Bill of Sale Sections 4.3 and 7 (Issues 3 and 4);
   - revising Section 11.12 so the SPA controls (Issues 3 and 4).
2. **Use the lease issue as leverage.** Seller's inability to satisfy Section 7.2(b) gives Gleidesk a strong reason to require the whole package as the price of closing. Send a reservation-of-rights notice promptly so the Section 8.1(c) cure clock can run well before the January 31, 2027 outside date.
3. **Get the following from the client:**
   - the history of the Section 9.3(c) and 9.4(d) insertion and any price trade-off;
   - the status of any contact with Pellucid, and the client's tolerance for relocation;
   - whether the client knew of the lease lapse at signing;
   - the client's appetite to terminate if Seller refuses the amendments.
4. **Due diligence follow-ups:**
   - Pull the actual Fresno lease and the First Amendment to confirm the notice mechanics.
   - Obtain a current lien search and DMV title search on the ten vehicles and on the equipment listed in Schedule 1.3.
   - Request a Closing-date update on the flashing-sealant remediation (about 80 installations outstanding as of September 30, 2026).

**Note on the September 2026 draft:** The September 24, 2026 draft is superseded and has no operative effect. I have cited it only as negotiation history for Issue 1. It is also relevant to Issue 2: its broader Section 6.4 ("timely exercise any renewal option") was drafted before the October 2 deadline passed, and the signed version lost the timing protection. All analysis above is based on the executed SPA, the Exhibit B form and the Disclosure Schedule.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Gleidesk Renewables Acquisition Corp. / Tenein Rooftop Solar, Inc. – Issues for pre-Closing attention

---

## 1. Bottom line

Gleidesk signed the Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA) on October 20, 2026. The deal has not closed, which gives Gleidesk its main leverage. Three problems need to be fixed before Closing:

1. **The Fresno Warehouse Lease renewal option has already lapsed.** The deadline was October 2, 2026, eighteen days before signing. Seller cannot perform SPA Section 6.4. The Fresno Warehouse is the Company's main inventory, fleet staging and dispatch facility, and the lease expires March 31, 2027.
2. **The Bill of Sale caps title claims on the Transferred Assets.** Bill of Sale Section 4.3 makes them "subject to the Cap" ($4,850,000). SPA Section 11.12 lets the Bill of Sale control as to Transferred Assets, so this likely overrides the Fundamental Representation carve-out in SPA Section 9.4(b).
3. **The Bill of Sale selects California law and Fresno County courts.** Through Section 11.12 again, this splits disputes away from the SPA's Delaware law and Court of Chancery forum.

Issues 2 and 3 both arise because SPA Section 11.12 gives the Bill of Sale priority. Fixing Section 11.12 addresses both at the root.

## 2. Key deal terms

| Term | Provision | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase Price | $48,500,000 | SPA §2.1 |
| Seller indemnity Cap | 10% of the Purchase Price ($4,850,000), applies to §9.2(a) and §9.2(d) claims | SPA §9.4(a) |
| Exclusions from Cap | Fundamental Representations (§§4.1, 4.2, 4.6 Title to Transferred Assets) and Fraud; capped instead at the Purchase Price (no cap for Fraud) | SPA §9.4(b) |
| Deductible | $485,000 (does not apply to Fundamental Representations or Fraud) | SPA §9.4(c) |
| Survival | 18 months after the Closing Date for general representations; Fundamental Representations and Taxes survive to the statute of limitations plus 60 days | SPA §9.1 |
| Governing law | State of Delaware | SPA §11.8 |
| Forum | Exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware | SPA §11.9 |
| Order of precedence | The Bill of Sale controls as to the Transferred Assets; otherwise the SPA controls over all other documents | SPA §11.12 |
| Outside date | January 31, 2027 | SPA §8.1(b) |

**Superseded draft.** The September 24, 2026 Buyer draft is superseded and is not operative. It is useful context on two points:

- It had **no** precedence clause equivalent to Section 11.12. That clause, and the Bill of Sale priority it creates, entered the deal after our draft.
- Its Section 6.4 required Seller to "timely exercise" the renewal option. The executed Section 6.4 requires exercise only "before the Closing."

---

## 3. Issues, ranked by significance

### Issue 1 – Fresno Warehouse Lease renewal window closed before signing

**Location:**
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.10(a), §8.1(d), (f) and (g)
- SPA Section 6.4
- Related: SPA Sections 4.10, 7.2(b) and 8.1(c)

**What the documents say:**
- The lease with Pellucid Logistics Park LLC expires **March 31, 2027**.
- The single five-year renewal option must be exercised by written notice "no later than one hundred eighty (180) days before the lease expiration date." If timely notice is not given, the option lapses.
- 180 days before March 31, 2027 is **October 2, 2026**.
- The schedule, dated October 20, 2026, states that "no renewal notice has been delivered."
- SPA Section 6.4 nonetheless requires Seller, before Closing, to cause the Company to exercise the option "in accordance with its terms" and to deliver the notice and any landlord acknowledgment.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **The option is gone.** On the lease terms as summarised, it lapsed before the SPA was signed. Seller cannot perform Section 6.4 by giving notice now. Any extension now depends entirely on Pellucid agreeing to one.
- **The operational exposure is serious.** The Fresno Warehouse is the Company's principal inventory, fleet staging and dispatch facility. It holds the Transferred Assets, including about $1.18 million of inverter and racking inventory and the warehouse equipment. Without action, Gleidesk could close and then lose the facility about two months later. It would then face relocation costs, business interruption, or a renewal at whatever rent Pellucid demands instead of the 95% of fair market rent under the option.
- **There is no rep-based claim.** Seller disclosed the lapse against Section 4.10, so a claim under Sections 4.10/9.2(a) is weak. The remedy runs through the covenant and the closing mechanics, and those only help **before** Closing.
- **Gleidesk has pre-Closing leverage.** Seller's non-performance of Section 6.4 means the closing condition in Section 7.2(b) (performance of covenants in all material respects) will not be satisfied. That supports a refusal to close and, after the 20-day cure period, termination under Section 8.1(c).
  - *Judgment call:* Seller may argue that a covenant impossible to perform at signing was never a real obligation, or that Buyer accepted the risk because the lapse was disclosed on the same day. Our better reading is that Seller took on an unconditional obligation and must deliver an extension or bear the consequences. The point is still arguable, so leverage should be used in negotiation rather than relied on as a sure walk right.

**Recommended fix (pursue now, before Closing):**
1. Require a **landlord-signed lease extension or amendment** (target: five years on the option economics) as an express closing condition. Add it to Section 7.2 by written amendment under Section 11.6.
2. If Pellucid will not sign before Closing, negotiate one or more fallbacks:
   - a **special indemnity**, outside the Cap and Deductible, for relocation, moving, fit-out, business interruption and any rent above the option rent;
   - an **escrow or holdback** to secure that indemnity;
   - a **purchase price reduction**.
3. Send Seller a written notice now under Sections 6.6 and 8.1(c) reserving Buyer's rights. Make clear that Gleidesk is not waiving the Section 7.2(b) condition. This preserves leverage and starts the cure clock if needed.
4. Obtain the actual Industrial Lease Agreement (March 15, 2022) and the First Amendment (January 9, 2024) from the data room. Disclosure Schedule §1.4 says the summaries are qualified by the underlying documents. We should confirm the notice deadline, any holdover terms, and whether the First Amendment changed renewal rights.

**Facts needed from the client:**
- How critical is Fresno to operations, and are there realistic alternative sites in the area?
- Has the business team been in contact with Pellucid?
- Is the outside date of January 31, 2027 workable if extension talks take time?

---

### Issue 2 – Bill of Sale subjects title claims to the Cap, overriding the SPA carve-out

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale (Exhibit B), Section 4.3 (Title Warranty)
- Read with SPA Sections 4.6, 9.4(a), 9.4(b) and 11.12

**What the documents say:**
- Under the SPA, Section 4.6 (Title to Transferred Assets) is a Fundamental Representation. Section 9.4(b) excludes it from the 10% Cap of $4,850,000 and from the Deductible. Title claims are capped only at the Purchase Price.
- Bill of Sale Section 4.3, however, states that Seller's liability for breach of its title warranties "is **subject to the Cap** set forth in Section 9.4(a) of the Purchase Agreement."
- Ordinarily the SPA would prevail over an ancillary document. Here, SPA Section 11.12 provides that "the Bill of Sale controls as to the Transferred Assets." Bill of Sale Section 6 reinforces this by tying itself to Section 11.12.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **The carve-out is likely lost.** Read together, these clauses likely remove the Fundamental Representation carve-out for title losses on the vehicles, inventory and warehouse equipment. Gleidesk's recovery for defective title or undisclosed liens on those assets would be limited to **$4,850,000**, not the Purchase Price.
- **Other claims compete for the same Cap.** The Cap is an aggregate limit shared with general rep claims under Section 9.2(a) and pre-Closing installation warranty claims under Section 9.2(d). Title losses would compete with those claims for the same $4.85 million, and could be squeezed out entirely if other claims use up the Cap first.
- **Lien risk is real.** The Company's Sierra Valley Commercial Bank credit facility is being paid off at Closing (Schedule 4.3 §4.2). Lender liens or third-party claims that reach Seller-owned vehicles or inventory are exactly the kind of exposure the carve-out was meant to protect.

**Judgment call:** Seller could argue there is no "conflict" for Section 11.12 purposes. On this view, the Bill of Sale warranty is a separate undertaking and Section 4.6 claims under the SPA remain uncapped. We should not rely on that argument. Section 11.12 gives the Bill of Sale priority "as to the Transferred Assets," and a court could readily treat Section 4.3 as governing all title claims on those assets. The allocated value of the Transferred Assets is about $2.6 million (Schedule 2.4). Whether the Cap actually bites therefore depends on lien and third-party claim exposure. The drafting risk is still not one Gleidesk should accept.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Bill of Sale Section 4.3:** delete "subject to the Cap set forth in Section 9.4(a)." Replace it with a statement that claims for breach of the title warranties are treated as claims under the Fundamental Representations, are excluded from the Cap and Deductible under Section 9.4(b), and survive as provided in Section 9.1.
- **And/or SPA Section 11.12:** amend so that the SPA controls over the Bill of Sale in all respects. The Bill of Sale would control only on the mechanics of conveyance. This also neutralises Issue 3.
- The Bill of Sale is still only a form and Seller signs it at Closing. Agreeing the revised form now, by SPA amendment under Section 11.6, avoids a Closing-day dispute.

---

### Issue 3 – Bill of Sale selects California law and a Fresno County forum

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale (Exhibit B), Section 7.1 and 7.2
- Read with SPA Sections 11.8, 11.9 and 11.12

**What the documents say:**
- The SPA is governed by **Delaware law** (Section 11.8). It places disputes in the exclusive jurisdiction of the **Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware** (Section 11.9).
- Bill of Sale Section 7.1 provides that the Bill of Sale, and all claims relating to the sale, conveyance and transfer of the Transferred Assets, are governed by the "**laws of the State of California**."
- Bill of Sale Section 7.2 submits the parties to the exclusive jurisdiction of the "state courts located in **Fresno County, California**."
- Because SPA Section 11.12 makes the Bill of Sale control as to the Transferred Assets, these provisions likely take effect.

**Why it matters to Gleidesk:**
- **A single dispute could be split across two forums.** Suppose a lien surfaces on a vehicle after Closing. The title and transfer claim would go to Fresno County under California law. A related indemnity claim under Article IX, and any claim under SPA Section 4.6, would go to the Court of Chancery under Delaware law.
- **The split creates practical risks:**
  - parallel proceedings and duplicated cost;
  - inconsistent results;
  - arguments over which court decides which issue;
  - uncertainty about whether the SPA's Section 11.10 jury waiver carries over, since pre-dispute jury waivers are generally not enforced in California courts.
- **It undercuts the Delaware choice** that Gleidesk, a Delaware buyer, negotiated.
- The interaction with Issue 2 compounds the risk. A California court applying California law would be construing the Bill of Sale's "subject to the Cap" language.

**Judgment call:** California law will necessarily govern some mechanical points, such as DMV registration and perhaps perfection of security interests in California-located goods. That does not require a California choice of law or forum for the contract claims. Please confirm with the client whether there was any business reason (for example, Seller convenience) for this clause, or whether it is simply form language that was never conformed.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Conform Bill of Sale Section 7** to SPA Sections 11.8–11.10: Delaware law, exclusive Court of Chancery jurisdiction with the same fallback courts, and a jury waiver.
- Alternatively, delete Section 7 and add a statement that the governing law, jurisdiction and jury waiver provisions of the SPA apply to the Bill of Sale.
- Make the Section 11.12 amendment described under Issue 2. With the SPA controlling, any remaining inconsistency resolves in favour of Delaware.

---

## 4. Suggested next steps

1. **This week:** obtain the Fresno lease and First Amendment from the data room, and send Seller a reservation-of-rights notice on Section 6.4.
2. **Client call:** confirm how critical Fresno is and what relocation alternatives exist; check whether there has been any contact with Pellucid; ask whether there is a business rationale for Bill of Sale Sections 4.3 and 7.
3. **Proposed SPA amendment (Section 11.6), as a single package for Seller:**
   - add a landlord-extension closing condition, or a special indemnity with escrow;
   - revise Section 11.12 so the SPA controls;
   - substitute a conformed Form of Bill of Sale with no Cap reference in Section 4.3 and Delaware law and forum in Section 7.
4. **Leverage:** Closing cannot occur until the Section 7.2 conditions are satisfied or waived. Gleidesk should not waive Section 7.2(b) or sign off on the Bill of Sale form until these points are resolved.
